entry.title: 260 Square Feet of Dead Air: Real Estate Finance, Club Goods, and the 24/7 Pool Room

link.title: 260 Square Feet of Dead Air: Real Estate Finance, Club Goods, and the 24/7 Pool Room

entry.content:
In Part 1 of this series, we looked at the microeconomics of the equipment in your hands: why a pool cue can cost anywhere from sub \$100 to over \$50,000, and how the market splits into utility tools and Veblen assets.

Today, we are zooming out from the stick to the room itself.

If you have lived in any major city over the last twenty years, you have likely watched your favorite traditional pool hall vanish—replaced by luxury apartments, a Sweetgreen, or a boutique fitness studio. Yet at the exact same time, a new breed of pool room is quietly booming in high rent cities from New York and Seattle to Taipei: the 24/7, unstaffed, keycard-access membership club.

As someone who researches real estate finance and economic theory—and spends way too many hours practicing 9-ball—this structural shift is fascinating. The death of the traditional urban pool hall and the rise of the automated “PropTech” billiards club is a masterclass in spatial unit economics, screening contracts, and the theory of club goods.

1. The Spatial Curse: The 58-Inch Stroke Tax

To understand why traditional pool halls struggle to survive modern urban retail rents, we have to start with the merciless math of commercial real estate: Revenue per Square Foot ($\text{Rev/SqFt}$).

A regulation 9-foot pool table (like a Diamond Pro-Am or Brunswick Gold Crown) has a playing surface of \$4.5\text{ ft} \times 9\text{ ft}$, or just 40.5 square feet. If you could pack pool tables edge-to-edge, billiards would be a goldmine.

Unfortunately, physics gets in the way. Because a standard pool cue is 58 inches long, players require roughly 5 feet of unobstructed clearance on all four sides of the table to take a full backswing. Once you add the table, the stroke perimeter, and minimal walkway clearance, a single 9-foot table consumes roughly $14\text{ ft} \times 18.5\text{ ft} \approx 260\text{ to }300\text{ square feet}$ of leasable floor space.

Think about the opportunity cost of 300 square feet in a commercial corridor:

  • A Restaurant or Bar: Fits 16 to 20 dining seats. Turning those seats 2.5 times an evening at a \$45 check generates \$1,800 to \$2,250 per night.
  • A Boutique Spin or Pilates Studio: Fits 12 reformer machines or bikes, generating \$35 per person per hour across multiple classes a day.
  • A 9-Foot Pool Table: Accommodates 2 people (maybe 4 in doubles) paying \$15 to \$20 per hour combined. Even across 6 peak evening hours, table time yields around \$100 a night—roughly \$0.33 per square foot per day.

In real estate finance terms, the air around a pool table is unmonetized dead space. When urban Triple-Net (NNN) retail rents climbed from $15/sq ft to \$45+/sq ft, pure table-time could no longer pay the landlord.

2. Adverse Selection and the Rothschild-Stiglitz Screening Problem

Historically, traditional pool halls solved the spatial math problem through cross-subsidization. Table time was treated as a break-even loss leader to anchor customers in the building while the house made its real margin selling high-markup beer, liquor, and fried food.

But relying on a Food & Beverage (F&B) cross-subsidy creates a textbook microeconomic pathology: adverse selection and misaligned incentives.

Consider the two archetypes walking into a pool hall:

  1. The Serious Grinder: Shows up on a Tuesday at 2:00 PM, rents a table for four hours, drinks free tap water, and demands pristine Simonis 860 cloth, clean Aramith balls, and tight pockets. F&B Margin: $0.
  2. The Friday Night Crowd: A group of six casual friends shows up at 10:00 PM, orders three pitchers of beer and nachos, hitting balls around pretty hard, sets sweating pint glasses on the rails or worse, the cloth, and occasionally rips the cloth attempting an illegal jump shot. F&B Margin: High. Equipment Depreciation: High.

To survive high ground-floor retail rent and pay for bartenders, kitchen staff, and bouncers, the traditional pool hall is forced to cater to the Friday night drinker. In doing so, the tables deteriorate, driving away the serious players.

How Membership Clubs Solve This: Screening Contracts

The modern 24/7 membership pool club flips this equilibrium on its head using one of the most famous mechanisms in microeconomics: Rothschild and Stiglitz’s (1976) model of Screening in Competitive Markets.

In a world of asymmetric information, a pool room owner cannot easily tell at the door whether a new customer is a respectful player or a cloth-ripping rowdy. So instead of policing behavior with security guards, the membership club offers a separating contract:

  • No bar, no kitchen, no single-hour walk-ins.
  • A flat \$150 to \$250 monthly recurring membership fee, plus an upfront onboarding orientation.

This contract acts as a pure self-selection screening device. A casual Friday night partier looking to drink beer and bang balls will never pay \$180/month for a quiet, alcohol-free room with etiquette rules, they self-select out to a sports bar or Topgolf. Conversely, the serious player who practices 15 hours a week views \$180/month as an absolute bargain.

3. Buchanan’s Theory of Clubs and Ostrom’s Commons

Once the membership model screens in the right cohort, how does an unstaffed room with \$10,000 Diamond tables survive 24 hours a day without someone stealing the balls or trashing the equipment?

This brings us to Nobel laureate James Buchanan’s (1965) An Economic Theory of Clubs and Elinor Ostrom’s (1990) Governing the Commons.

In public economics, goods exist on a spectrum between pure private goods and pure public goods. A membership pool hall is the literal textbook definition of a Buchanan Club Good: it is excludable (via smartphone smart-lock at the door), and non-rivalrous up to a congestion threshold (as long as one of the 8 tables is open, my practice session doesn’t hurt yours).

Buchanan showed that the optimal size of a club ($N^*$) is where the marginal benefit of adding one more member (sharing the fixed real estate lease across more wallets) equals the marginal congestion cost (the probability of showing up at 7:00 PM and having to wait for a table).

Furthermore, transforming customers from hourly spot-market renters into club members eliminates moral hazard:

  • In a traditional hall, an hourly renter faces a classic Tragedy of the Commons—they have zero financial or social stake in whether the cloth is brushed or chalk is left face-down on the rails.
  • In a capped 80-member club governed by Ostrom-style community norms (backed by cloud cameras and keycard access logs), members actively brush the tables, clean the balls, and police the space themselves because they share ownership of the club’s quality.

4. PropTech Arbitrage and “Paying Not to Go to the Gym”

Finally, look at the corporate finance transformation on the income statement. By combining the Club Good model with simple PropTech automation—an app-based smart lock, security cameras, and IoT relay switches that automatically flip on the overhead perimeter LED light when a member reserves a table—the business model achieves three massive financial advantages:

  1. Spatial Arbitrage (Class-A Felt in Class-C Space): Because members navigate to the club intentionally via an app rather than wandering in off the street, the club does not need expensive ground-floor retail visibility. It can lease windowless 2nd-floor Class B/C office space, basement footprints, or light-industrial flex space at 40% to 60% lower rent per square foot—Wait, no windows? For serious pool players, zero sunlight glare on the table is a feature, not a bug!
  2. CapEx-for-OpEx Labor Substitution: In a traditional mid-sized room, front-desk and bar payroll consumes 30% to 45% of gross revenue, bleeding cash during dead weekday afternoons. Automation drops on-site variable labor near zero, unlocking 168 hours per week of asset utilization so night-owl grinders can practice at 2:30 AM at zero marginal cost to the owner.
  3. Cash Flow Smoothing & DellaVigna-Malmendier Breakage: As DellaVigna and Malmendier (2006) famously documented in Paying Not to Go to the Gym, flat monthly subscription contracts bundle predictable recurring revenue for the operator with behavioral “breakage” from members who travel or get busy at work for three weeks but keep their membership active to hold their spot on the roster. Fixed lease obligations are covered on the 1st of every month.

Visualizing the Unit Economics: Why Traditional Halls Get Squeezed

To see why this shift is inevitable in high-rent cities, let’s plot the monthly Net Operating Income (NOI) of two rooms across rising commercial real estate rents:

  • Model A (Traditional 12-Table Retail Hall): 4,500 sq ft (needs bar/lounge area), ground-floor retail rent, staffed 84 hours/week ($11,500/mo payroll), earning hourly table time + F&B margin.
  • Model B (24/7 Self-Serve 8-Table Membership Club): 2,400 sq ft, 2nd-floor/flex space (receiving a 40% spatial arbitrage discount on baseline street rent), 75 members paying \$175/mo, automated smart locks/lights (\$800/mo part-time cleaning/maintenance).

entry.title: The $50,000 Stick: What Pool Cues Teach Us About Economics

link.title: The $50,000 Stick: What Pool Cues Teach Us About Economics

entry.content:
As a pool player and a financial economist, I have always found the economics of pool fascinating. So, I am starting this series to look at the economics of pool, beginning with a piece of equipment that defies almost every logical rule of the modern sports market.

Imagine the finals of a World 9-Ball Championship. The lights are hot, the crowd is silent, and hundreds of thousands of dollars (\$250,000 to the winner!) are on the line. When a player steps up to the table to face a table-length tough shot, you would expect them to be holding the absolute pinnacle of modern sports engineering, likely a lab tested, carbon fiber cue provided by a massive corporate sponsor.

But for years, if you watched World Champions like Taiwan’s Ko Pin-yi or his brothers, you would see something completely different.

Before their recent sponsorship deals, the Ko brothers were famously not sponsored by cue makers, stepping up to the biggest shots of their lives holding traditional Southwest cues. They were leaving lucrative cue sponsorship money on the table, bypassing mathematically “perfect” low deflection technology, to play with a traditional wooden custom cue.

In almost any other sport, this is unthinkable. A PGA Tour golfer does not turn down a TaylorMade sponsorship to play with a wooden driver they bought themselves.

But billiards is not like other sports. The Ko brothers played with Southwest cues for a very specific reason: the subjective, tactile feedback known in the pool world simply as “the hit.”

This introduces the central paradox of the billiards market. It is a space where the line between a highly engineered athletic tool and an artisan masterpiece is entirely blurred. As a result, the price range for pool cues is wider than any other sports equipment I can think of. A functional, mass-produced Chinese cue will cost you \$100 to \$200. A reputable professional brand with state-of-the-art technology maxes out around \$1,000. But if you want a custom Southwest, or a masterpiece from a maker like Zen or Black Boar? You are looking at waitlists spanning a decade and price tags ranging from \$10,000 to over \$50,000.

Economic Principle 1: The Staircase of Diminishing Returns

In Intro to Economics, the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns is always drawn as a smooth, continuous hill. Every additional dollar you spend is supposed to give you a slightly smaller, continuous boost in performance.

If you actually play pool, you know the cue market doesn’t work like that at all. Instead of a smooth curve, pool cues follow a step-function technology frontier separated by flat plateaus where your money buys little extra performance.

Stage 1A: The First \$100 (Basic Mechanical Competence) Moving from a warped bar cue without a usable tip[ to a $100 entry-level cue like a Viking Valhalla or a McDermott Lucky yields the steepest return on investment in billiards. That first hundred dollars buys baseline mechanical competence: a straight maple shaft, a respectable single-layer leather tip, and a solid joint. At this stage, every dollar directly eliminates equipment-induced misses.

Stage 1B: The Budget Low-Deflection Entry Point (\$100–\$300) Unlike what a casual player might assume, measurable quality continues to climb past the $100 mark up to around \$250–\$300, epitomized by cues like the Cuetec AVID series, or entry level carbon cues like Rhino or Raven. Moving from a \$100 Lucky to a ~\$275 Cuetec AVID Chroma or Rhino isn’t just cosmetic, it unlocks entry-level low-deflection (LD) technology, making side spin application easier. You get a glass-bonded, vacuum sealed maple shaft with a lightened front end cavity on the avid or an entry level carbon fiber shaft from Rhino or Raven, that reduces cue-ball deflection on spin shots, paired with a multi-layered laminated tip (like a Tiger Everest) and a stiffer, warp-resistant construction.

Plateau 1: The “Dead Zone” (\$300–\$600) Once you reach a Cuetec AVID or equivalent budget LD cue around \$275, the objective performance curve hits a sudden wall. What happens if you spend \$450 or \$550 on an upgraded traditional cue? From a physics standpoint, almost nothing.

In fact, a \$475 Cuetec AVID Opt-X uses the exact same \$159 shaft as the \$280 AVID Chroma. Because the next leap in shaft R&D (aerospace carbon fiber) is an “indivisible good”—you can’t buy half a carbon-fiber tube—every extra dollar spent between \$300 and \$600 goes almost entirely toward cosmetic product differentiation: fancier decals, painted points, or better wraps.

Stage 2: The Carbon Fiber Jump (\$600–\$1,000) To get another measurable boost in performance, you have to jump across the cosmetic plateau into the \$600 to \$1,000 bracket.

At \$600 to \$700, you unlock full carbon-fiber setups or advanced shafts like the Cuetec SVB Gen 1 (Cynergy), Bull Carbon, or McDermott Defy, climbing up to around \$1,000 for an entry level Predator cue with a REVO shaft or a Mezz Ignite setup. Here, your money is buying aerospace grade carbon composite, radial consistency that never warps, and ultra low front-end mass that maximizes force transfer and minimizes deflection.

Plateau 2: The “Feel” Regime (\$1,000–\$5,000) Once you cross \$1,000, measurable objective performance hits a hard ceiling. Spending \$2,500 on a cue will not make the shaft deflect any less or the tip hold chalk any better. From \$1,000 to \$5,000, marginal dollars go toward subjective feel: balance points, exotic wood cores, joint pin stiffness, acoustic resonance, and intricate inlays instead of decals.

The Art & Asset Frontier (\$5,000–\$50,000+) Once we cross \$5,000 into the realm of Southwest, Black Boar, or a \$40,000 Zen cue, we have left the sports equipment market entirely. These are functional art pieces and Veblen goods, governed by scarcity, decade-long waitlists, and artisan prestige rather than shot-making physics.

The Exception: Subjective Utility and “The Hit”

Just when you think a \$10,000 cue is purely about conspicuous consumption, we must return to the Ko brothers.

In Asian pool culture, particularly in Taiwan, custom cues are often considered superior for high-level play. While Western players rely heavily on the objective engineering of carbon fiber, Taiwanese coaches often argue that mass produced shafts lack “stopping power” or the solid feedback required for absolute elite cue ball control.

This introduces the economic concept of Subjective Utility. While a carbon fiber Predator can prove its low deflection with physics and data, the “hit” of an ebony Southwest provides a tactile feedback that elite players genuinely believe gives them a competitive edge. When a professional player feels they can control the cue ball 1% better because of how the wood resonates in their grip, that \$10,000 price tag isn’t conspicuous consumption anymore—it is a functional investment in their livelihood.

Economic Principle 2: Waitlist Arbitrage and Alternative Assets

If you look closely at the secondary market for custom cues, you realize that a \$10,000 Southwest or a \$40,000 Zen isn’t priced like sports equipment at all—it is priced like a financial asset.

Consider the supply dynamics of Southwest Cues. Operating out of a small shop in Las Vegas, they refuse to scale up into mass production, resulting in perfectly inelastic supply. Today, the waitlist to buy a cue directly from Southwest is over 18 to 20 years long. Because the shop prices their cues below the true market-clearing equilibrium, getting your name on the waitlist is effectively acquiring a long-dated, deep-in-the-money call option. The day a buyer finally pays the retail price and takes delivery of their cue, they can immediately flip it on the secondary market for two to three times what they paid—a textbook example of waitlist arbitrage and economic rent.

Furthermore, because the secondary market is decentralized, it faces what Nobel laureate George Akerlof called the “Market for Lemons”, information asymmetry where buyers fear counterfeits or hidden defects. To prevent market collapse, custom cue makers have built institutional trust mechanisms. Southwest stamps a unique 7 digit serial number onto the brass joint pin of every cue and issues official Letters of Authenticity for any Southwest cues in circulation, functioning like a micro central bank verifying its own currency.

The Two Economies of the Pool Hall

Ultimately, the extreme price curve of pool cues exists because the billiards market is actually two completely different economies sharing the same pool tables:

  1. The Utility Economy (\$100–\$1000): Governed by engineering, R&D competition, and diminishing marginal returns. A \$550 carbon fiber shaft is a depreciating consumer durable—you buy it to pocket balls, and like a smartphone or a golf driver, it loses resale value the moment you chalk it.
  2. The Asset & Artisan Economy (\$5,000–\$50,000+): Governed by inelastic supply, Veblen signaling, subjective utility, and scarcity. A custom cue from a famous maker is an appreciating alternative asset, more akin to a Patek Philippe watch, a 1959 Gibson Les Paul, or a Carlo Bugatti designed furniture, than a tennis racket.

Whether a player chooses a lab engineered carbon fiber shaft or waits fifteen years for a piece of hand turned wood comes down to what they are really optimizing for: minimizing cue ball deflection, chasing the elusive feel of “the hit,” or holding a piece of functional art that appreciates between racks.

Visualize the Market: Performance vs. Price

entry.title: Coq au Vin for a group

link.title: Coq au Vin for a group

entry.content:
Coq au Vin

A rustic French chicken braise made for feeding a crowd. Boneless chicken thighs soak overnight in red wine, then are browned in bacon fat and slowly braised with aromatic vegetables. The sauce is finished with beurre manié for a glossy, velvety consistency.

Ingredients

Chicken and Marinade

  • 6–8 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs
  • 1 bottle red wine (750 ml), or enough to surround the chicken in the marinating bag
  • Fresh thyme or rosemary, optional

Braising Base

  • ½ lb bacon, diced (use more for a richer, smokier flavor)
  • 3 yellow onions, diced
  • 3 carrots, diced, or more to taste
  • 6–8 garlic cloves, minced
  • 2 tbsp tomato paste
  • Chicken stock, approximately half the volume of wine used, as needed
  • 2–3 bay leaves, optional
  • Dried thyme or other herbs, to taste
  • Salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • All-purpose flour, optional, for dredging the chicken

Beurre Manié

  • 2 tbsp softened unsalted butter
  • 2 tbsp all-purpose flour

To Finish

  • Reserved crispy bacon
  • Fresh parsley or other fresh herbs, chopped

Instructions

1. Marinate the chicken

Place the chicken thighs in a large food-safe zip-top bag. Pour in the red wine, adding enough to surround the chicken. Add fresh thyme or rosemary if desired.

Seal the bag, place it in a dish to catch any leaks, and refrigerate overnight.

2. Render the bacon

Remove the chicken from the marinade, reserving the wine. Pat the chicken thoroughly dry with paper towels.

In a large Dutch oven or heavy-bottomed pot, cook the diced bacon over medium heat until crisp and the fat has rendered. Remove the bacon with a slotted spoon and reserve it for serving. Leave the rendered fat in the pot.

3. Brown the chicken

Season the chicken with salt and pepper. If desired, lightly dredge the thighs in flour, shaking off the excess.

Working in batches, brown the chicken in the bacon fat until golden on the outside. Avoid overcrowding the pot; depending on its size and your stove, this may take four or more batches.

Transfer the browned chicken to a tray or plate. It does not need to be cooked through yet.

4. Build the aromatic base

Add the onions and carrots to the same pot. Cook until they begin to soften, scraping up the browned bits from the bottom.

Add the garlic and cook until fragrant. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for another minute or two.

Deglaze with chicken stock, scraping the bottom of the pot to release the fond.

5. Reduce the wine

Meanwhile, pour the reserved marinade into a separate saucepan. Bring it to a full boil, then simmer until reduced by approximately half and slightly syrupy.

Because the wine was in contact with raw chicken, it must be thoroughly boiled before being incorporated into the braise.

6. Braise the chicken

Pour the reduced wine into the Dutch oven. Return the browned chicken and any accumulated juices to the pot.

Add bay leaves, dried thyme, or other herbs as desired. Add chicken stock, starting at roughly half the volume of wine used, and adjust as needed so the chicken is surrounded by enough braising liquid.

Bring to a gentle simmer. Cover with a lid or use a cartouche to regulate evaporation.

Braise for approximately 30–40 minutes, or until the chicken is tender and fully cooked. Check that the thickest pieces reach at least 165°F (74°C).

7. Finish the sauce with beurre manié

Remove the chicken temporarily and keep it warm. Discard the bay leaves.

In a small bowl, mash the softened butter and flour together with a fork until a smooth paste forms.

Bring the braising liquid to a gentle simmer. Whisk in the beurre manié a little at a time, allowing each addition to dissolve before adding more. Simmer for several minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens and loses its raw-flour taste.

Use only as much beurre manié as needed to achieve a rich, velvety sauce. Return the chicken to the pot and gently warm through.

Taste and adjust the seasoning.

8. Garnish and serve

Serve directly from the Dutch oven or transfer to a large serving dish. Scatter the reserved crispy bacon over the chicken and finish with chopped fresh parsley or other fresh herbs.

Serve with mashed potatoes, buttered noodles, or crusty bread to soak up the sauce.

Notes

  • Wine: Côtes du Rhône is a dependable choice. Pinot Noir or Beaujolais also work well. Choose a dry wine you would enjoy drinking.
  • Chicken cuts: Boneless thighs make serving a crowd convenient. Bone-in thighs or drumsticks work too, but require additional cooking time.
  • Gluten-free: Skip the flour dredge and replace the flour-based beurre manié with a suitable gluten-free thickener.
  • Make ahead: The braise can be made ahead and gently reheated. The sauce may thicken in the refrigerator; loosen it with a splash of stock when reheating.
  • Leftovers: Refrigerate promptly and consume within 3–4 days.

entry.title: a post with marimo snippets
entry.content:
marimo notebooks can run Python directly in the reader’s browser. Opt a page in from its front matter:

---
layout: post
title: a post with marimo snippets
marimo: true
---

Nothing is loaded on pages without that flag, so bundling the plugin costs nothing site-wide.

Runnable snippets

Wrap fenced Python blocks in a container and the runtime turns them into an interactive notebook after the page loads:

import marimo as mo

slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 20, value=5, label="n")
slider

mo.md(f"The first {slider.value} squares: {[i**2 for i in range(1, slider.value + 1)]}")

Until the runtime has moved those blocks into place the container stays hidden, so readers never see the raw source flash before it becomes a notebook.

Embedding a hosted notebook

If you already publish a notebook — on marimo.app or your own WASM host — embed it instead:

{% al_marimo_embed src="https://marimo.app/l/your-notebook" height="700px" caption="Sampling demo" %}

The frame is sandboxed without allow-same-origin, so the embedded notebook cannot reach this page’s storage or cookies.

A note on what this loads

The marimo-snippets runtime is vendored into the plugin at a pinned version and served from your own site, rather than pulled from a CDN — so no third-party origin executes script in your readers’ pages. Running a notebook does contact marimo’s host, which is worth knowing before you opt a page in.

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. entry.content:
This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

First tabs

To add tabs, use the following syntax:

{% tabs group-name %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-1 %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php
  • js
  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

  • A quote

  • Hipster list

    • brunch
    • fixie
    • raybans
    • messenger bag

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

entry.title: a post with vega lite
entry.content:
This is an example post with some vega lite code.

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}
```

Which generates:
